title: MB7-05377
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, his spouse XXXX XXXX XXXX and their three minor daughters, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, all citizens of Mexico, are appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) to reject their refugee protection claim.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, his spouse XXXX XXXX XXXX and their three minor daughters, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, all citizens of Mexico, are appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) to reject their refugee protection claim.
They are not submitting any new evidence in their appeal and are not requesting that a hearing be held before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).
The female appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, was appointed the designated representative of the three minor daughters.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD, namely, that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX are neither "Convention refugees" under section 96 of the IRPA nor "persons in need of protection" under section 97 of the IRPA.
In the Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form) that he filed before the RPD, the principal appellant alleges that he was extorted by criminals while working as a bus driver in XXXX.

He alleges that he was beaten on XXXX XXXX, 2016, by these criminals, who accused him of not having given them money for the two preceeding weeks. He alleges that his spouse received a telephone call faking his kidnapping on XXXX XXXX, 2016.
On XXXX XXXX, 2016, the appellants left Mexico for Canada, where they claimed refugee protection.
The female appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, and the minor appellants are basing their claim on that of the principal appellant.
The RPD rejected the refugee protection claim on the basis that the male appellant's allegations were not credible.
Before the RAD, the appellants submit that the RPD erred in its assessment of their credibility, for reasons that will be detailed later in the "Analysis" section, if necessary.

For these reasons, the appellants are asking the RAD to set aside the determination of the RPD and grant them refugee protection, or, alternitavely, to refer the matter to the RPD for re-determination. STANDARD OF REVIEW AND THE ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

The RAD's role is to review RPD decisions using the correctness standard of review after conducting its own analysis of the record in order to determine whether the RPD erred, as submitted by the appellant. The exception to this rule concerns the RPD's findings in the assessment of the credibility of or the weight to be given to the oral evidence it hears, in cases where it enjoys a meaningful advantage. The RAD then owes a measure of deference to the RPD's findings (Canada v. Huruglica, F.C.A., No. A-470-14). In my analysis, I will provide reasons if I find that the RPD had a meaningful advantage.
The issue in this case is whether the RPD erred in its assessment of the appellants' credibility.
In my opinion, the answer to this question is no, for the following reasons.
The RPD based its decision on the following elements: A. The principal appellant's testimony about his work was vague.

He was unable to explain simple elements such as his salary, his hours and who determined his schedule. Furthermore, he testified that he had a special driver's licence authorizing him to drive a bus, while the licence he filed in evidence indicates that he can only drive private vehicles.

Listening to the recording of the hearing before the RPD, I come to the same conclusion as the latter on this subject. The male appellant's testimony was vague in that he was unable to explain the conditions of his alleged job as a bus driver, such as the name of his employer, his co-workers, his hours, his salary, and who or what determines his schedule.

I also find that, contrary to his testimony, his driver's licence indicates that he can only drive private vehicles. The principal claimant stated that he was [translation] "mixed up." In my opinion, this explanation is not reasonable in the context of this case.

Not only does the male appellant not have the driver's licence authorizing him to drive a bus, but he also did not file any other official document that could establish his job as a bus driver, which he alleges to have had since 2003. The attestation filed as Exhibit D-3 (page 268 of the RPD record) is just a letter, without letterhead, from a source unknown to the panel, and it is therefore insufficient to support the male appellant's allegations, given his vague and contradictory testimony. B. It is implausible that the principal appellant could have driven a bus for 13 years without the required licence.

As the RPD concluded, I am of the opinion that it is implausible that the male appellant could have driven a bus without the required licence and that neither his employer nor his insurance company ever required him to obtain it.

When asked what happened when he had to produce his driver's licence to the police, the male appellant responded that he has never had to do so in all his career. Again, like the RPD, I am of the opinion that it is unlikely that the male appellant has never had to show his licence to authorities during these 13 years. C. It is not credible that the male appellant never spoke to his employer about his alleged problems and never asked to change his schedule.

When asked whether he spoke to his employer about his problems, the male appellant answered [translation] "No, why?" In my opinion, this response already undermines the male appellant's credibility: it seems logical to me to discuss the extortion problem with his employer, either to try to manage the problem, to discuss possible ways to get protection, or to simply change his schedule. On that point, the male appellant stated that [translation] "there is no other schedule." When he was asked to explain why there was no other schedule at his work, the male appellant responded that it is because his employer had never changed his schedule since he started working for him. In my opinion, this explanation is neither logical nor reasonable.

Moreover, the male appellant filed Exhibit D-2 (page 257 of the RPD record) into evidence, which is allegedly a letter from a co-worker. In my opinion, this letter adds to the confusion of the male appellant's testimony. The letter is allegedly from a co-worker, even though the male appellant testified that he had only one co-worker whose name he does not know; the author of this letter seems familiar with the male appellant's problems, even though he testified that he never spoke about them; the letter seems to mention several colleagues (the author uses [translation] "we") and refers to the "taxi base," not buses; the author also filed a copy of his driver's licence in evidence, which indicates that he is authorized to drive buses, contrary to the male appellant's licence. D. The RPD identifies a number of other elements that undermine the male appellant's credibility.

For example, the fact that he does not know the name of his insurance company; the fact that he alleges that his attackers knew [translation] "all about him," yet they did not know his name and still allegedly found his personal contact information; the fact that he testified that he met his attackers three times before changing his answer to six times when confronted with his BOC Form; the fact that he alleged that the police were accomplices to the criminals without a reasonable explanation for the basis of this statement.

In my opinion, these elements considered seperately are not fatal to the claim; however, when considered together with elements A through D mentioned above, I find that there is sufficient evidence to undermine the credibility of the appellant's central allegations.
In their memorandum, the appellants submit that the RPD erred by not considering the Mexican context in which the alleged events happened.

In my opinion, this context cannot, however, explain the contradictions and inconsistencies noted. The male appellant did not explain at the hearing or in his appeal memorandum how the Mexican context could justify the contradictions, inconsistencies, and vague and imprecise nature of his testimony.
Consequently, in light of the foregoing, I find that the appellants failed to establish that the RPD committed errors warranting the RAD's intervention.

For these reasons, I confirm the determination of the RPD, namely, that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX are neither "Convention refugees" under section 96 of the IRPA nor "persons in need of protection" withing the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA.

The appeal is dismissed. Normand Leduc Normand Leduc January 23, 2019 Date IRB translation Original language: French 2 RAD.25.02 (April 9, 2013) Disponible en français RAD File No. / No de dossier de la SAR MB7-05377 / MB7-05378 MB7-05379 / MB7-05380 / MB7-05381 4
